Idaho Crystal Peak (gone) is about 1.5 km from the Crystal Ridge coordinates. No new photos with usable URLs were found.
Consistent, well-documented staffing history and an active-use status make this one of the more straightforward entries. Only wrinkle is the 1932 vs 1933 build-year discrepancy, noted in the story.

Brief design L-4 is the 1935 cab; corrected to R-6 for the current cab. Brief height_m 6.1 kept; sources disagree (20 ft vs 15 ft). Brief agency Idaho Department of Lands is confirmed. Staffing is volunteer-based; the Idaho Fire Lookouts page is dated 2021. Access and rental status are not stated. Keeping Watch (University of Idaho) and an IDL page were seen in search results but not read. Brief elevation_m 1919.6 agrees with the register's 6,298 ft (1,920 m).

Staffing is disputed: firelookout.com and Daytrip Northwest say staffed every summer, Trails Off Road says unmanned, and none is dated. The brief's height_m 3.0 has no source among the pages read, so it is omitted. The 1994 SITPA history names a Sunset Mtn. lookout but gives no location; the story flags the uncertainty rather than linking it. No rental listing turned up; no Boise NF or recreation.gov page was read. The event dated 1940 is a SITPA-era event that may belong to another mountain.

No source gives a specific year staffing ended; firelookout.com's 'emergency status for several years' phrasing was used as-is. Sources conflict on tower height (20ft vs 30ft) -- flagged in resolved_conflicts and in the story rather than resolved. Removed an unsupported 'network'/'Upper St. Joe country' characterization and an unsupported 1930s-1960s service-span claim from the story; neither was backed by a source quote.

Build year of current cab disputed (1954 vs 1958). Date staffing ended not found in sources. Brief's kind 'ground' fits the 1922 cabin; the current cab sits on a concrete base and the Forest Lookouts page calls it two-story, so consider kind two_story. No fire at this lookout was found. No rental found. The 1958 'Swan Home' clipping on the Forest Lookouts page is a different place and was not used. The FS page says 'Last updated September 21, 2026' and carries a header notice 'UPDATED Sept. 19 - Crooked Fire Area, Road, and Trail Closure'; the notice does not name this site, so the reason for the site closure is not confirmed. The Forest Lookouts page is the only source with clippings for the 1920s to 1940s staffing.

The NHLR coordinates (N 43.306, W 111.921) fall outside Lemhi County and do not match the brief's lat/lon (44.885, -114.216). The Rex's page location (24 miles southwest of Salmon) fits the brief's coordinates, so the brief's coordinates were left alone; the NHLR coordinates look wrong. The elevation conflict (7,414 vs 9,960 ft) is not settled; check USGS before relying on either. Access and permission are not stated on any page read. Read budget used: the Trailforks trail page returned HTTP 403.

Current status is not confirmed. A search result titled 'Thorn Creek Butte Lookout Tower [CLOSED]' on AllTrails could not be opened (HTTP 403), so it is not relied on; verify before any visit. No Forest Service page for this lookout was found. Not on the FFLA rentals list as far as the grep showed. The 1974-1982 staffing dates are the only dated staffing. The brief's access 'unknown' is now 'restricted' on the basis of the sources' emergency-only language, which is a judgement call. A 2026 Crooked Fire closure near Idaho City appeared in search results but was not checked against this site.

Build dates conflict: 1962 (NHLR field, firelookout.com, Idaho Fire Lookouts) versus 1962 or 1965 (NHLR description) and 1965 (Forest Lookouts). Cupola date 1933 versus 1922. Elevation 8,656 ft (NHLR) versus 8652 ft (firelookout.com). Staffing is seasonal and undated. No notable fire was recorded in the pages read. The brief's events for 1962 and the 2020 registration are supported. One search snippet, not read, described a jeep trail to within about 5 miles of the summit; it is unverified and not used. Current 2026 access was not confirmed.

Staffing is dated: Idaho Fire Lookouts gives a page date of September 3, 2021 and a staff list running to approximate 2008 to 2023, so current staffing may differ. Access level is not stated on any page read; the story asks visitors to get permission first. The brief's height_m 3.0 is the 10-foot base only and is proposed for removal. The 1922 vs 1956 build-year conflict is recorded in resolved_conflicts.

The brief's height_m 1.8 has no source among the pages read, so it is omitted. Concrete base 1950 (NHLR, Idaho Fire Lookouts) versus 1956 (firelookout.com). Elevation 8,082 ft (NHLR) versus 8086 ft (firelookout.com, Idaho Fire Lookouts). The association's name is spelled Protection on the NHLR and Protective elsewhere; the story uses Protective. Current staffing is unconfirmed: the association's undated employment page names only Brundage and Lookout mountains. No closure or rental notice was found. The brief's events for 1921, 1977 and 2020 are supported.

Three conflicts need an editor's call: the 1932 structure (L-4 vs R-1), the 1964 base (concrete vs cinder-block), and elevation (10,337 vs 10,394 ft). Current staffing is contested. Access is set to public on the Chamber's visitor listing; the cab's interior is not described, so confirm with Salmon-Challis NF before treating the cab as open. The brief's height_m of 3.0 is the base height, not total height. No rental found. The FS page names three staffed lookouts and does not name Twin Peaks, but it does not say which unstaffed lookouts remain.

Record's built year 1828 is a typo in NHLR's data field; 1928 is used. Sources disagree on end of use: Idaho Fire Lookouts says abandoned 1968, Forest Fire Lookout says not used since the 1970s. The cabin burning in 2012 rests on Forest Fire Lookout alone; the Idaho writer's 2012 photos show the cabin still standing. Access is unknown. The tower has broken ladder rungs and missing platforms; the story does not encourage climbing. Forest name differs between sources (Salmon vs Salmon-Challis). Idaho Fire Lookouts post dated January 16, 2023. Staffing history rests on that one site.
Brief's location conflict (NHLR vs RIDB coordinates, a few hundred meters apart) not addressed here since it concerns map data, not the narrative. No new photos found.

Elevation conflict: NHLR says 5,890 ft; three other sources say 5,981 ft. Correction proposed, editor to confirm. The 1968 date is the current structure; earlier lookouts from the 1920s, 1932 and 1934 are noted but the 1920s date is only a decade. Only two staff names are on record (1974, 1977). Rental status is disputed (Forest Service list vs two web sources). The Hike-In Emergency tag is read from the Idaho Fire Lookouts header. No height_m in the record; sources give a 10-ft tower. Post dated October 2, 2025.

Build year conflicts (1931 first tower vs NHLR 1961) and the staffing schedule differ across sources. A WebSearch snippet mentions a 2000 Burgdorf Junction Fire spotting role and fire-wrapping; not verified on a fetched page, so left out. Current record height_m 3.0 is the ten-foot block base, not total height. Access left restricted; no source documents public climbing or rental.

Fixes to the record: height_m 9.1 is the 1931 pole tower; the current 53-ft tower is about 16.2 m. Access moved from unknown to closed per the Forest Service page (updated 2025-02-19); the search snippet of a camping listing and a trail guide were not read and are left out. The 1931 pole-tower height appears as 30 ft in NHLR and Idaho Fire Lookouts. No documented staffing history exists. The earlier fs.fed.us URL in the queue record does not resolve; the fs.usda.gov page was used instead. The 16 vs 38 mile discrepancy from Pierce is unresolved and reported as such.

Tower standing, cabin gone, lower stairs removed, climbing not safe (Idaho Fire Lookouts). Abandonment has no exact year; sources say the 1950s. Only two named lookouts: L.L. Hydron (1935, secondhand via Idaho Fire Lookouts' citation of the Bonners Ferry Herald) and Burt Callahan (1936). Forest name differs between NHLR/FS (Idaho Panhandle) and Idaho Fire Lookouts (Kaniksu). Record access 'unknown' is now public trail access; the tower is not to be climbed. Build year: 1934 vs 1934 or 1935.

No source read supports an access level (public, restricted or otherwise), so the access key is omitted. Staffing is seasonal per firelookout.com, undated. Build year 1933 (three sources) vs 1934 (one). Register date 2011 (NHLR) vs 2020 (Idaho Fire Lookouts). Known-staff names come from one site only. Record access 'unknown' should stay unless the Boise National Forest answers. No rental found. Record fields otherwise match the sources.

Access 'public' rests on one map site (TopoZone) plus the 2016 visit report; treat it as provisional and check with the Challis National Forest. Build year 1935 (four sources) vs 1936 (Idaho). Elevation 9,556 vs 9,546 ft. Staffing end 1943 (TopoZone) vs 1946 abandonment. Record coordinates match NHLR and TopoZone; the record's conflict note about Idaho Fire Lookouts coordinates (about 0.5 km off) is not visible in the pages read. Cabin is a ground cab, not a tower. No rental found.

Access 'restricted' is inferred from the Forest Service's active-lookout and respect-the-space wording; no source says the cab is closed to visitors, so the story says so. Elevation: the record's elevation_m 2085.4 follows NHLR (6,842 ft); the Forest Service gives 6,826 ft (about 2080.6 m). Editor to decide whether to change it; not proposed as a correction. The 2006 crash is relayed secondhand through Idaho Fire Lookouts from a Forest Service Facebook post, which was not fetched directly. Staffing 2026 is from the trailhead page's last update (May 2026). No rental found.

The NRHP nomination (Schroeder, 2002) was not readable; the catalog.archives.gov PDF returned no extractable text, so NRHP details come from Wikipedia. Build year (1934 vs 1936-1938) and height (80 vs 100 ft) conflict across sources. The closed status comes from Clio's reading of a park map and should be checked with the park office. The 2017 visit report is the most recent condition evidence found.

Built 1935 by CCC is supported by two sources (NHLR and a hobby site repeating the Living New Deal date). The brief's record had no built event; this adds it. The 2009 restoration money is spelled AARA in the sources and ARRA in the brief record; the story uses the sources' spelling. Current climbing permission is unconfirmed: the only climbing statement is a hobby site, and the DNR map gives no tower rule. Height and staffing dates are not in any source read. Agency is recorded as Indiana Department of Conservation per the Forest Lookouts header; that is an older name and the DNR map is the current state publisher, so check the agency field before publishing.

Build date disputed (1935 completion vs a 1935 to 1952 window). Access 'closed' rests on a June 2022 map legend read by Indiana Fire Towers; no current access source found. A Forest Lookouts page also quotes a December 31, 1938 Vincennes Sun Commercial item about a tower 'being re-erected near Stendal' in Pike County State Forest; the item does not name Hartwell, so it is not used. Living New Deal returned HTTP 403 and was not used. Grokipedia was not used.

The DNR closure notice is undated in the cache, so the closed status is as of the last read and should be rechecked before publication. The May 2025 fire comes from Facebook posts cited by a personal enthusiast site; the story attributes it to that site. The brief's height_m of 12.2 m is not supported by any source read. Indiana Fire Towers also describes a personal climb in 2021; that is not used and is not encouraged. The 1989 accident report is not in the story because it does not name this tower. The old NHLR Lookout.aspx page returned HTTP 500 and was not used. One websearch.py search was run. Fact-check 2026-10-08: the 1927 two-tower statement is now shown with the geodetic-survey context from the same page; the observer detail keeps the fall-and-spring qualifier; the still-standing and not-climbable status is footnoted.

Current public access/climbability status is unclear from sources consulted; the brief's record also listed access as 'unknown' which matches. Wikipedia's claims are cited to a single footnote source [1] on that page which was not independently retrieved here; treated as generally reliable given specificity but flagged for anyone who wants to verify the underlying reference.

Location and access disputed: The Outbound says the tower was moved to Brown County State Park and can be climbed; Indiana Fire Towers and the register say it stands on IU land with no public access. The story does not encourage climbing. Build year (1930 register vs 1931 contemporary sources) and height (75 vs 80 ft) also disputed. Nothing found on staffing or notable fires.

Only two readable sources. The build year is disputed: NHLR says 1935, while Mark A's wall photo note (circa 1937) and the 1936 map point later. A Living New Deal search snippet gives 1934, but that page returned HTTP 403 and is not cited. An AP/Herald-Times search snippet describes the tower reopening after a decades-long closure, but that page returned HTTP 403 and no closure or reopening is cited here, so an editor should check it by hand. The brief's access 'unknown' can be updated to public (NHLR, as of 2025). No staffing history was found in the readable sources.

The brief's agency 'State Forest' is not an agency, and none of the readable sources names the agency that administers this tower, so the agency fact is left out. The access level 'restricted' rests on Mark A's note that the gate is usually locked; the Visit Bloomington post says the tower is available again. The 2026 'restored' event is dated only by the April 2026 post, so its year may not match the renovation. No Living New Deal or Facebook sources were checked for this tower.

Record height 30.5 m (100 ft) corrected to 26.2 m (86 ft) per NHLR and Indiana Landmarks. Living New Deal (about 100 ft, completed 1934) and Wikipedia (90 ft) appeared only in search results and were not read; not used. Clio is a student-created entry (2020) that cites WBIW Aug 2020, not read; its reopening date and closure length are reported as Clio's claims. Access marked public from Clio and Indiana Landmarks; no current park page on hours or climbing was read. NHLR visit form leaves the staffing question unanswered. Current elevation_m 234.7 matches NHLR 770 ft (235 m). No new photos added.

Construction sequence before 1941 is disputed between the NHLR (CCC 1937, fire, 1941 rebuild) and the sign and hobbyist survey (1932 erected). Staffing, fire year and official access status were not found in the pages read. Climbability rests on one hobbyist site and needs confirmation with the state park. Living New Deal page returned 403; Wikipedia O'Bannon Woods page had no tower text in the fetched output. Agency left out because the NHLR administered-by value did not appear in the fetched text.

The 1935 vs 1939 build date is unresolved. A Living New Deal search snippet and a Facebook snippet (CCC Camp S-93, 1935-1936) were seen only as search results, not read, so they are not cited. The brief's access 'unknown' can be updated to public (reopened 2019). OpenStreetMap tags height=30.5 and access=yes, but the OSM text splits the tag values across lines, so OSM is not quoted; height_m 30.5 is supported by the 100-foot figure in Indiana Landmarks. Current climbing status rests on Mark A's undated notes. The brief's 'Well's County' spelling is an OSM variant.

Record height 27.4 m (90 ft) is corrected to 24.4 m (80 ft) per the register and 1932 steel-tower reports, but the 1946 NGS description says about 108 ft, so the height is not settled. The builder is disputed: the register says CCC 1931-35, the hobbyist survey quotes a wooden tower first and a later CCC steel tower. The 1932 site is also described two ways: about 1.5 miles south of Brownstown (Sept 1932 article) and about 2.5 miles (NGS). The 2010 restoration line on the eastern lookouts page has no source of its own. The climbable claim rests only on a hobbyist site; the story does not encourage climbing. Staffing in 1932 was an announced plan, not a confirmed record. No notable fire tied to the tower was found in these sources. The 1970 staffed_last year is a placeholder for 'the 1970s'. Record access was 'unknown' and is now public, supported by the register and the DNR page. Search budget: one websearch.py call.

Build year is 1927 by the 1928 report (quoted by NHLR) and a July 1927 photo; the sign says the 1930s. The plan report that announced the tower is dated 1926 by the Register and hobby site but 1923 by the Forest Lookouts transcription; the story reports both. Height is 80 ft as built per the 1928 report, but the Register and a 1941 item say 90 ft or more; the record's 24.4 m is kept but may be revisited. Climbing: the hobby site says the cab is not open and the tower can be climbed partway; no official rule found, so the story does not encourage climbing. The 1944 staffing and radio items come from a Brown County Democrat clipping transcribed on the Forest Lookouts page; the clipping itself was not read. Restoration status: fundraising announced January 2026; no evidence of work started. Agency: Indiana DNR per NHLR; the Forest Lookouts header uses the older Department of Conservation name. Fire history: no specific fires found.

Build year is disputed: 1931 delivery (newspaper), 1932 (register), 1933 completion (county survey quoted on a hobbyist site). The record has no build year, so none is written to facts. The Living New Deal page refused access (HTTP 403), so it is not cited. The hobbyist climbability claim is not confirmed by the state; the story does not encourage climbing. The DNR page says Martin State Forest was established in 1932 while the hobbyist site says acquired 1933; that concerns the forest, not the tower, and is not reconciled. Current condition beyond the hobbyist note is unknown. Search budget: two websearch.py calls. The 'standing' and 'climbable' notes come from one hobbyist page and are not state confirmation.

NHLR is a solid primary source with direct site-visit detail (trail distance, ranger anecdote, climbable status). The weebly compendium corroborates WPA construction and park location but differs on the year by three years; could not resolve which is more authoritative within budget. No source addresses overnight rental, so the story states the absence of any such record rather than asserting it is unavailable.

Builder, cab material and abandonment date are disputed; the 35-foot figure looks like an error. Access 'public' rests on The Outbound's hike notes (undated) and the county's rental post; confirm with Route 377 before any visit advice goes out. Staffing comes from NHLR visit reports dated 2008, 2016 and 2022. No photos recorded. The county's 'replace with steel' wording is quoted as printed.

Demolition rests on the NHLR and FFLOS registers, which are the same organization's two sites, and is dated only 'as of 2024'. The 2016 newspaper is the only independent source. The 1934 build is supported by three sources. No lookout names, staffing dates or notable fires were found. The 'abandoned' step has no year, so it is left out of events. Brief status 'standing' is corrected to removed.

Elevation not in facts. The brief gives 384.4 m, but LEX18 says the highest point in Bath County is 1,388 feet (about 423 m); the two should be checked against a survey before either is used. The 1959 rebuild comes from one source (Eastern lookouts history) and is worded as 'half the original height' without detail. The tower 'fell out of use in the 1970s' is a decade only, so no event year is given. NHLR 'Staffed? No' is undated, so staffing as_of uses the check date. The USFS recarea page in the brief (recid=70728) does not mention Tater Knob, so the 2008 Forest Service statement is taken from its quotation on NHLR. Read budget ran over (about 7 page reads) because the first two fetches were low-yield.

Very thin sourcing. No entry for Fields Fire Tower in the cached NHLR or FFLOS (firetower.org) Louisiana registers, and no mention in the cached centraluslookouts.com Louisiana page beyond a bare county-header photo callout with no text. Wikipedia's own citation for 'still standing' points to a USGS GNIS feature-detail page (geonames.usgs.gov, Apex app); it is JavaScript-rendered and returned only the generic USGS/Board on Geographic Names homepage when fetched, so it could not be used directly. One WebSearch and two page reads were spent (this Wikipedia page plus the dead-end GNIS fetch); stopped researching rather than spend more of the budget chasing a page that would not render. Builder, construction date, design, height, and managing agency are all unknown and should not be guessed. A human with access to LDAF's Louisiana Statewide Forest Resource Assessment and Strategy PDF (cited elsewhere in the same Wikipedia list, pp. 36-37) might find more.

No build year, first-staffing date, or move/alteration history was found in the sources reached, so the story says so. The record's elevation (27.1 m) is consistent with the register's 89 ft. The 33.5 m height is converted from the register's 110 ft. Access is unknown: no source reached says whether the public may visit, so no access or visit fact is written. Use wording conflicts between the register (very high fire danger days) and Wikipedia (high wind days); the Wikipedia asterisk is unexplained. Do not confuse with a Gordon tower in Wisconsin (a 1935 Aermotor listing seen in a search result, T.44N-R.12W); that is a different structure and was excluded. An OpenStreetMap node (358380019) tags it as an observation tower of lattice construction at ~26 m, but that was not cited. Search budget: three websearch.py calls, one over the two-per-tower budget.

Thin on the tower itself: the register page is the only source about the tower; the 2010 NRHP nomination and the NPS page cover the recreation area and say the CCC built the tower only 'likely'. No staffing, current access or post-2011 condition was found, so access and staffing are left out of facts. The firemen's dwelling dates (1935-1958) belong to the cabin, not the tower. The register says 'CCC Troop F-6' and the NPS page says 'Company 5407, Camp F-6'; the story flags this without merging them as fact. Not used: the register gives the recreation area's NRHP listing as December 2011, while Wikipedia gives December 7, 2010 citing the NPS weekly list; this concerns the recreation area, not the tower. The nhlr.org Lookout.aspx?id=906 page returned HTTP 500. Used about 10 distinct pages, over the 6-read budget, because the tower has few sources.

Unresolved conflict: the register says a 99 ft 9 in Aermotor LX-25 built in 1933 (with a 1934 USFS photo and a 1952 stair change); the central Louisiana lookouts site says an 82-ft steel tower with a 7x7 cab was erected in 1951-52. It may be a replacement or a different tower. The Forest History Society PDF 'A History of Kisatchie' was searched by keyword and did not yield a Kisatchie-tower entry. No source found on current access or climbability; the access level is left out of facts. The Wikipedia 'active use' status is undated. The record's height_m 25.0 conflicts with the register.

The register's only removal date is 'by 2021'. Wikipedia's Merryville row estimates removal between 2015 and 2016 from old aerial imagery; this fits 'by 2021' but is not confirmed, so no removal year is certain. No built year beyond 'early 1950s', so no built event was entered. No staffing, fire or access information found in the sources read; the Central US Lookouts Merryville page is only a heading. The record's status 'standing' is contradicted by both registers and Wikipedia (proposed correction). The Wikipedia 'Torn down.' quote is taken from the Merryville row of the list.

Two independent sources (the NHLR register and a lookout-hobbyist history site) agree and complement each other, but neither confirms what happened after the 2006 disassembly: whether restoration was completed, where the tower now physically stands, or whether it's accessible. The tower record's coordinates are tagged 'exact' from NHLR but almost certainly predate the 2006 move. Worth a human follow-up with the Catahoula Ranger District or a recent visit report before treating location/access as current.

Height and cab design are unconfirmed. A search snippet from the FFLA Massachusetts chapter gives 68 ft, but the Facebook post could not be read, so it is not used. The register names the older Bureau of Forest Fire Control as administrator; the 2023 Gazette names DCR, so agency is set to DCR and the record's agency field may need updating. Staffing: the register's 'Staffed seasonally' note is undated; the 2023 staffing item is a plan. The closure comment is undated (photo April 2016), so current access should be confirmed. Climbing rests on one 2020 trip report. No fire credited to this tower was found. The Eastern US Lookouts Moores Hill page yielded only navigation text.

NHLR and the 1915 Boston Daily Globe item disagree on when the first Barden Hill tower went up (1913 vs. apparently still 'planned' in March 1915); kept both in the story rather than picking one. No source found addresses current staffing, access, or climbability, so those stay unknown in the tower record. The easternuslookouts.weebly.com page carries a banner image but it isn't clearly captioned as depicting this specific tower, so it was not added to photos.

Removal in 2003 is well supported (register, Forest Lookouts, Willhite). Unresolved: first tower 1915 vs 1918; 1970 tower height 40 ft vs possibly 60 ft; 1970 vs 1971 completion (a Facebook search snippet from FFLA Massachusetts says 1971, not read). Staffing history is taken from the register and Willhite only; the 1947 observer is named in Willhite and in a 1947 newspaper quoted on Forest Lookouts. Leads not read: 2006 Mount Everett summit resource management plan on mass.gov (mentions a 2000 proposal to repair the tower). Access is public trail access; no tower to climb.

The brief's record puts the FFLOS registration (US 1548, MA 55, March 27, 2014) on the Pine Hill tower, but that entry is the former Manomet Hill site; see corrections. Access is not recorded as a fact: no current access rules were found, and the 2014 NHLR visit report says directions are not signed. The story advises checking with the Bureau before any visit and does not tell readers to climb or not to climb. Build year: the NHLR and FFLOS say 1966. A search snippet from an FFLA Massachusetts Facebook post gives 1969 and says the tower is Plymouth's fifth; the page itself returned no text, so the date is not cited and should be checked if it matters. Mass.gov returned HTTP 403 and firelookout.org's Plymouth pages returned 404, so the state's current staffing and access status could not be checked. The brief's elevation_m (114.3) matches the NHLR 375 ft (114 m). The height of 21.3 m is the NHLR 70-ft figure for the current tower, which the brief did not list. Fact-check 2026-10-08: the story's 'record' wording is corrected to the register's 'activity', 'went up' is corrected to 'moved' for the 1939 Telegraph Hill tower, the 1942 new-tower versus relocated-from-Pelham disagreement is now stated, and the unsupported 'do not climb the tower without permission' line was removed because the NHLR page has no climbing or permission text.

Unresolved: the 1920 replacement tower is 68 ft iron per the register, 71 ft per a Aug 1919 newspaper item, and 70 ft steel per a 1919 state report. Access is disputed: Pioneer Valley says open to the public; a 2018 hiker found the top locked; the 2016 register visit reports say staffed only in fire-danger periods. Access level is set to restricted as a judgment call and should be checked with DCR. Agency: the register says Mass. Bureau of Forest Fire Control while Pioneer Valley calls the forest a DCR property; the register wording is kept. Elevation 488.3 m (1,602 ft) is the register's figure; Wikipedia gives 1,617 ft and Pioneer Valley gives DCR's 1,621 ft for the summit, so the record was not changed. A Pioneer Valley photo credit (Aug 2013, CC BY-SA 3.0) is noted but no image URL was found, so no photo entry. Two FFLA Massachusetts Facebook posts (1922 and 1920s photos) appeared in search results only and were not read.

Staffing conflict is unresolved: NHLR says rangers staff it during high fire danger (present tense); NPS says it has not been manned since 1976. The NPS fire towers page was last updated 2020-10-07. Current 2024-2026 opening status was not confirmed by any source I could read. OpenStreetMap node 358231332 tags access=private, which conflicts with NPS; not used. Wikidata gives elevation 833 ft; NHLR gives 807 ft (246 m, matching the brief). Coordinates match NHLR. Registration date September 16, 1993 is confirmed by NHLR and NPS.

Sources disagree on several dates and on what was moved. Staffing end: WMTW says 1976, Maine Memory says the tower closed in 1968. Move: WMTW says the cab went to the visitor center in 2011 by helicopter; Maine Geographic says the tower was reassembled in 2015; Maine Memory says October 2012 to the Natural Resource Education Center. The register's 1959 date for the present steel tower conflicts with 1919 elsewhere. The register entry (US 67) still describes the summit site, not Greenville. Agency for the Greenville tower is not documented (the register lists the Maine Dept. of Conservation for the summit site), so it is left out. The NREC page (nrecmoosehead.org) returned 404 and was not used. Access is marked public only because the tower sits beside a visitor center that Maine Geographic calls worth a visit; climbing is not documented. The Commons photo already in the record was not re-added. Page reads: about 6 distinct pages, plus one search.

Only source found is the Eastern US Lookouts page, which itself just quotes a 1929 newspaper item and the 1967-68 Forest Commissioner's biennial report. No NHLR or FFLOS register page exists for this site (nhlr.org returned 404), and nothing was found on current status, access, staffing, or whether the tower still stands. The tower record's location (45.65887, -68.18754, from FFLA) was not independently corroborated against the 1929 'Macwahoc Plantation' description within this budget; worth a closer look if a human researcher has more time.

Sources disagree on early dates and on the tower's history. (1) First towers: Wikipedia says 1936 and the NRHP nomination ties them to the 1936 fire without a year; the NPS Isle Royale page says CCC built them in 1939. (2) Old tower: Wikipedia says it stood near the new site and was torn down in 1963; the nomination puts it a half-mile away on Turkey Ridge. (3) Naming: the NPS Isle Royale page calls the re-established Turkey Ridge tower 'Feldtmann Tower'; the nomination uses New Feldtmann Fire Tower for the 1964 tower. Check which tower the Park Service means before any visit. (4) Height: the record's 12.2 m (40 ft, from NHLR) matches the 1961 plan; the built tower is 41 ft 3 in per the nomination and Wikipedia. Proposed correction to 12.6 m. (5) Abandonment: Wikipedia says by 1968; the nomination says use diminished after 1968 and eventually ended, with shelter use into the 1980s. (6) Access: climbing partway is from the NPS places page (updated Feb 2022); the NPS fire-tower page says the tower is no longer utilized. Current conditions and any closure are unverified. The NRHP nomination PDF is long; only targeted extracts were read, so the 1936 construction year for the old towers is not confirmed in the nomination itself. Reads: 5 distinct web pages plus one search; a local cache copy of an eastern lookouts list was checked and not used.

Built-year conflict (1936 vs. NHLR's 1940/CCC claim) is real and unresolved; I favored 1936 since both Wikipedia and the NRHP period of significance back it, but a human with access to the actual NRHP nomination PDF (not just the NPGallery detail page) could settle it outright. No cached local source pages existed for this tower beyond the NHLR page; no newspaper or Forest Service primary-source search was attempted beyond the two WebFetch calls used here (within the 3-search budget, no WebSearch calls were needed since WebFetch on known URLs sufficed).

No source gives a build year, builder, or the tower's original agency/duty near Isle, or when it stopped serving as a working lookout before the 1981 move. The FFLA state list (cached) and Wikidata both just confirm name, location, county, and 'standing' status, with no narrative detail. Height (100 ft) and the 1981 move date are corroborated by multiple independent sources (Exploration Vacation, Mpls.St.Paul Magazine, and MN DNR), which is why confidence is medium rather than low despite the record itself being nearly empty. Fact-check 2026-10-04: the draft stated the tower is "steel" and has an "enclosed" platform, and gave the moraine/dam description in wording copied almost verbatim from the DNR/mspmag pages; none of the cited sources mention the tower's material or an enclosed platform, so those were removed, the moraine sentence was rewritten in original wording, and the Isle origin claim's footnote was corrected to the sources that actually say "near Isle" (Exploration Vacation and DNR, not mspmag).

Build year is disputed (1934 NHLR vs 1935 nomination and county). Current access comes from a 2026 visitor guide and was not checked on site. Staffing status rests on a 2019 article. The NRHP listing date was not confirmed.

No 2024-2026 report on condition, climbing rules or closure was found after two searches. Access was left out because no source supports a level. Coordinates conflict: NHLR gives 32 19' 27 N, 89 30' 19 W (matches the brief); Wikipedia gives 32 24' 14 N, 89 28' 01 W, about 10 km away. The Wikipedia coordinates were not used. The NRHP form was prepared in 1998 by Todd Sanders and was signed by the Deputy SHPO on 10/27/98, with a site visit on September 27, 1997. The Shockaloo relocation claim comes from one lookout history site and is contradicted in part by the NRHP nomination. Unresolved.

Only substantive source found was the NHLR register page (cached locally); no FFLOS page, newspaper, NRHP nomination, or Forest Service history turned up for this specific tower in two WebSearch queries plus WebFetch checks (anyplaceamerica.com 403'd; Wikipedia's Woodland, MS article has nothing on the tower). No build year, staffing, or fire history available. Fact-check pass removed two unsupported details from the story: a claim that the tower sits near a 'small community of Woodland' (not stated on the NHLR page) and an attribution of the 2022 site visit to 'NHLR volunteers' specifically (the register page records only that a site visit occurred, not who performed it). All other claims verified directly against the cached NHLR page and the Wikipedia Mississippi Forestry Commission article.
Build-year conflict between sources on whether the present cab is 1929 or 1930; both likely refer to the same rebuild after the 1929 fire. No staffing history found for this tower.

Only four sources, one of them an undated station description (the source of the staffing and access route). No notable fires, builder, or reason for construction found in the sources. The 'access' level was changed from 'restricted' to 'unknown': that was an inference from the reservation location and the wire gate, and the sources give no visiting rules. The contact-the-tribe advice had no source and was removed from the story. The brief's claim that firelookout.com is missing from its own standing map was not verified. One WebSearch found no new Badger-specific sources.

The history (about 1910 pole platform, 1927 cabin, 1957 tower) agrees across all three sources. Height conflict: NHLR and firelookout.com say 30 feet, Recreation.gov says 26 feet. Elevation: NHLR says 6,531 ft (1,991 m); Recreation.gov and firelookout.com say 6,529 ft. The record uses the brief's elevation of 1990.6 m. No staffing information and no notable fires appear in these three sources. Firelookout.com credits photos to the U.S. Forest Service and Gary Weber, but no image URLs were read, so none are recorded. Reservation dates should be checked on Recreation.gov before publishing.

Stair status after rehabilitation is unconfirmed; NHLR says the lower stairs were removed in 2005 and no source I read says they were replaced. Completion year is unclear: NHLR says fall 2013 and also lists volunteer staffing from 2012. Search summaries (not cited, not verified) said the tower returned to service in 2012 and was staffed by volunteers 2012-2017 and by a Forest Service employee from 2018. The Forest Service PDF named in the brief (stelprd3792970.pdf) returned 404 and was not used. The NHLR page links a Bob Marshall Wilderness Complex newsletter on the renovations; it is a lead for the stair and completion question. The height correction (3.7 m to 9.1 m) rests on firelookout.com alone. Coordinates match NHLR. The Flathead Beacon source spells the lookout 'Baptise' (typo kept in the quote).

Two sources agree on the 1922 cabin, the 1934 or 1930s L-4 tower, and the 1962 cab. Staffing and the active-service status are undated, so the current status is medium confidence. The access level was changed from 'restricted' to 'unknown': that was inferred from the active lookout service, and the sources give no visiting rules. The visiting-advice sentence had no source and was removed from the story. The brief's height of 3.0 m is the concrete base, not the overall height. Photos are credited to the Fire Lookout Museum, USFS and Gary Weber, but no image URLs were found, so none are listed. The brief's 'two_story' kind describes the 1922 cabin, not the present structure.

Build history conflicts: NHLR says a camp in 1928 then the L-4 in 1933, while a 1931 clipping says a smoke chaser occupied the Bear Top lookout before the 1932 house. Name variants: Beartop, Bear Top, Bare Top, Bare mountain. No source found for current staffing, rental or visiting status; the register's 'usually staffed' line is undated. The FFLA Facebook post did not load. The Hiking Project trail is not confirmed as the route to the lookout. Pages read: 5 (firelookout, montanalookouts, NHLR, FS cabin page, Hiking Project). Search: 2 queries.

Built dates 1931, 1940 and 1965 agree across NHLR, firelookout.com and the Weebly history. The 2017 PDF's roof and assessment lines are not quotable: pdftotext duplicates every line, so check_quotes cannot match them, and the story leaves them out. Current tower condition rests on one Forest Service sentence about restoration. The brief's 2017 'restored' event is overstated (see corrections). Elevation disagrees by about 114 ft between sources. Trail access is public; nothing supports climbing the tower and the story says so.

Reasonably well documented for a rental-program lookout: two independent narrative sources (National Forest Foundation, Western News) corroborate the NHLR/firelookout.com build history. The 1980s retirement from fire duty comes from the National Forest Foundation piece; the 1984 rental start and the builder's name (Stef Ludvikson, for both the 1928 cabin and the 1934 tower) come only from the Western News article — NHLR and firelookout.com do not name a builder, so that attribution rests on a single source. Two small, unresolved conflicts flagged above: the cabin's build year (1928 vs 1929) and the summit elevation (three different figures across sources). A third, odder wrinkle: the National Forest Foundation piece implies the log cabin standing near the tower today was moved to the site in the 1950s to replace a deteriorated building, which sits awkwardly against the 1928/1929 'first structure, still there' framing from NHLR and firelookout.com — the story notes this rather than resolving it. The Purcell Mountains location also comes only from the National Forest Foundation piece. No NRHP nomination form or newspaper archive hit was found in the search budget; a Chronicling America or Montana Memory Project search might turn up more on the 1934 or 1966 construction if someone wants to dig further.

No newspaper or NRHP nomination form located; the 1984 date is NRHP-eligibility, not a formal National Register listing, and the story is careful to say so. Two official-ish sources (Recreation.gov listing vs. the Forest Service's own Lolo NF page) disagree slightly on the lookout's water source: non-potable spring 3/4 mile downhill vs. a filterable spring 0.5 mile away. Wikipedia's 'Big Hole Lookout' article was used only to find the underlying USFS citation (fs.usda.gov/r01/lolo/recreation/big-hole-lookout), not cited directly, per the guide. Record's existing 'design' field was null; proposed a correction above. One WebSearch call used, plus WebFetch on two known URLs. Fact-check pass (2026-10-04): firelookout.com actually lists the elevation as 6919 ft, not 6,922 ft, so that figure is now cited to NHLR alone; the 'Cabinet National Forest' detail and the precise staffed-to-1972 date are not on firelookout.com or NHLR's visible text respectively and were re-cited to the sources that actually state them (Recreation.gov and the USFS Lolo NF page); a missing footnote on the cabin's furnishings/vault-toilet sentence was added.

Blue Mountain (Kootenai NF, Libby) is a different site from other Blue Mountain lookouts in Montana, so keep the Libby identity and the NHLR number US 342, MT 24. Height conflicts (72 vs 80 ft). Current staffing and access are unconfirmed: firelookout.com is undated and describes summer staffing, and a travel blog with no visible date describes a host trailer and a rough road. The Kootenai camping-and-cabins page excerpt I read does not list Blue Mountain, but the list was partial, so rental status is left unstated. No notable fire at the site appears in these sources. The 2020 PDF could not be quote-checked because its extracted text is duplicated, so the 2020 assessment is in events without a quote.

Access level omitted: the register gives no access rule, and the 2013 KGVO report is the only road description. No staffing key: the register calls it active, undated. Elevation not used: the register gives 1,940 m, and a search summary gave a different figure I could not confirm on a fetched page. A search summary mentioned a 37-year lookout staffer; it was not on any fetched page, so it is left out. Film-date conflict is unresolved and flagged in the story.

Built year (1937) and L-4 design agree across sources, so confidence on those is high. Current condition is the weak point: no source found is dated after the 2003 restoration, and firelookout.com's 'presently abandoned' note is undated. The nomination's condition description has no date in the text I read. Location: the record uses the NHLR point (45.83737, -114.28933); the RIDB point (45.82449, -114.29445) in the record is about 1.5 km away. Not resolved; a human should check which point is right. Elevation: 7,688 ft (NHLR) vs 7,753 ft (firelookout.com); the record's 2343.3 m follows NHLR. NRHP listing date not confirmed: I did not read the NPGallery listing record for a date; search snippets suggest 2018 but are unverified, so no listing-date event was written. Staffing ended 'mid-1980s' (approximate year 1985). The 1958 start of the staff list is the first name listed on firelookout.com; staff names are deliberately not reproduced.

Thin record: the register has no description, firelookout.com has one line, and the Montana list confirms standing status and register numbers. Searches for fires, staffing, design and height found nothing for this tower. The brief's access value 'permission' has no supporting source, so it is proposed as unknown and omitted from facts. Coordinates, county, 1930 build, 2022 registration and elevation (1,433 m) match the register. Story length is set by this evidence.

No access level: nothing fetched says whether the tower can be entered. Staffing conflict is unresolved; the 2016 report is the only dated staffing source (its 2014 sister report was not read). Brief's R-6 design belongs to the 1968 tower; the 1933 first tower was L-4. Trail facts come from a Seeley Lake visitor page on the Rumble Creek Lakes hike, not a Forest Service source. A 1956 Forest Service photo caption mentions a Condon lookout tower but cannot be tied to Cooney, so it is omitted. Height 30 ft converted to 9.1 m.

NPGallery asset page metadata was readable but the full nomination narrative PDF text did not come through in the grep; architect name (Clyde Fickes) and significance period are confirmed from the metadata fields themselves. No new photos found.

Structure and dates are well corroborated (NHLR and firelookout.com agree). Staffing evidence is dated (2014 guide) or undated (NHLR); the Trekking Wild visit is undated. No fire history, NRHP nomination or rental listing found. Elevation not used: NHLR gives 6,028 ft, firelookout gives 6031 ft. Verify current season and cab access with the Flathead National Forest before publishing.

No source gives an original construction/first-staffed date before the 1958 relocation, or details on specific notable fires fought from this lookout. 'Yager' vs 'Yeager' Butte spelling differs between NHLR and Recreation.gov; story uses both forms once. firelookout.com (source 3) duplicates NHLR's text nearly verbatim, so it was used only to corroborate, not as an independent source.

Brief's existing record (built 1933, L-4, 6.1m height) is consistent with Recreation.gov/firelookout.com; only NHLR's page gives 1932 instead, so the story reports the one-year discrepancy rather than silently picking a side. NRHP reference number 100002041 taken from the brief's register field, which matches NHLR's own cross-reference. No newspaper coverage or NRHP nomination PDF was consulted; confidence is high because three independent, consistent descriptive sources exist even though they disagree on the exact year.

Built year: the register's 1970 and the sources' 1935 cabin are both correct for different structures, so the story gives both. Staffing: 'staffed every summer' appears on the register and the tribal page, but neither page is dated, so the 2022 as_of was removed (it was the register's registration year). Height: the record's 4.3 m conflicts with the 20-ft tower the sources describe (proposed correction, not applied). Access: administered by the tribes on the reservation; no public visiting arrangement was found, and the story says to check with the tribe first. Elevation difference is under 10 ft. Nominator and lookout staff names are deliberately omitted. The 1979 and 1994 items come from a secondary history site quoting a newspaper and a newsletter; the originals were not checked.

Build year 1953 is well corroborated across NHLR, firelookout.com and 1952-1953 newspaper items quoted on the Forest Lookouts page. Staffing is only described as summer and is undated. The Moss Mountain Inn guide is a lodging site's hiking article and its road-access and gate details are undated. No fire history or rental listing found. Verify current access and staffing with the Flathead National Forest. Brief record fields (design L-4, 1953 build, 2011 registration) are supported, so no corrections proposed.

No source gives an end date for staffed fire-watch duty, or names any specific fire spotted from Garnet Mountain. The brief's record flags a build-year conflict across sources, but all three sources checked here agree on the same build sequence (1930 camp / 1950 cab / 1962 cab), so no conflict was found in what we read; it's possible the flagged conflict is against a source not checked in this pass (e.g. an NRHP nomination). Fact-check 2026-10-04: the draft misstated Garnet Mountain as sitting 'in the Gallatin Range' -- source 2 lists the Gallatin Range only as a feature visible to the south, not the mountain's own range, so the story was corrected to list it alongside the other viewed features. Two footnote citations were also wrong: the 1950 secondhand-cab/Lincoln Mountain sentence had cited source 2 (Recreation.gov), which says nothing about that history, instead of source 3 (firelookout.com); and the 'one of the more popular lookouts' claim, which comes only from source 3's wording, had been attached to sources 1 and 2.

Brief's 'height_m: 1.8' field looks like an error or placeholder (1.8m is under 6 feet, implausible for any lookout tower; rec.gov says the current tower is 40 feet tall). Flagging as a possible data issue for the editor rather than a sourced correction, since no source gives a tower height in meters directly. Built-year conflict (1963 vs 1964 for the current tower) handled as the brief's note anticipated.

Two independent, detailed sources agree closely on the build history (1921 rag outfit -> 1939 L-4 on 20-ft pole tower -> 1964 R-6 flattop on 30-ft timber tower) and on staffing into the 1970s. Flagged a likely height_m error in the tower record (20 ft vs. the current 30-ft tower). Minor elevation discrepancy not flagged: NHLR gives 6,029 ft (1,838 m, matches record); firelookout.com gives 6,092 ft -- not material enough for a correction. Did not need to use the web-search budget; both cached pages were sufficient. Fact-check 2026-10-04: removed an uncited 'Clark Fork River country' detail from the opening sentence (not in either source) and rewrote two sentences that too closely copied source wording ('rag outfit' tent description; 'without permanent living quarters' line). Spot-checked the NHLR registry-number/date quote and both firelookout.com quotes (location and named personnel) directly against fetch_text.py output; all three matched the source exactly.

Construction, design and CCC attribution rest on the NRHP nomination (stated as belief). The brief lists NRHP 100002297 as a register; the nomination file calls the lookout eligible for listing. I did not confirm a listing date or final status, so the story says eligible. The last staffing year is not exact (firelookout.com says into the 1980s; NHLR calls it inactive in 1984). The rental is current per the Forest Service page (undated). Brief record fields (1939 build, L-4 design, 2003 registration) are supported, so no corrections proposed.

Elevation differs notably between NHLR (6,887 ft / 2,099 m, matching the brief's elevation_m field) and Recreation.gov (7,587 ft) -- flagged in the story rather than silently picking one, since neither page explains the gap and it's larger than a rounding difference. Build-year conflict between firelookout.com (1934/1954) and NHLR+Recreation.gov (1932/1962) also flagged; went with the two-source majority for the main narrative. No staffing-end date is corroborated outside firelookout.com, so that claim is attributed to it alone. No NRHP nomination PDF or newspaper source found in two web searches; confidence is medium given the unresolved elevation and date conflicts.

Construction history is well documented (NRHP nomination and NPS planning file). Current condition and access rest on 2012-era sources; no 2026 source was found. Elevation conflict: NHLR gives 6,810 ft (2,076 m), which matches the brief's 2075.7 m; firelookout.com gives 7244 ft. Not used in the story. The NPS planning file's date is not shown in the fetched text. The Wikipedia Built 1945 infobox matches the nomination. Pages read: 6 (NHLR, Wikipedia, firelookout, NRHP PDF, Whitefish Pilot, NPS planning PDF). Search: 1 query.

Build year is the main conflict: 1869 (firelookout.com), 1874 (Montana Free Press), 1876 (register and Visit Helena listing). The brief's record of 1876 is kept. Restoration cost and start month conflict as noted. The year 2025 for the restoration is inferred: the Free Press story is dated April 7, 2025 and says the work was expected to finish by the end of May, and KTVH does not print a year. The city's restoration project page (helenamt.gov) returned no text. Whether the public may climb the tower is unknown. Pages read: 6 (NHLR, Visit Helena listing, firelookout.com, Montana Free Press, mthistory.org, KTVH). Search: 1 query.

No fire at this site appears in the sources read. The brief's kind two_story is not verified: NHLR describes an L-4 cab on a one-story concrete base, and a search snippet quoting a firelookout.org directory (not read) called it a two-story cab. Left unchanged. Consider whether the 1954 event should be replaced rather than built. Staffing and current access are unconfirmed; no Forest Service page was read. One WebSearch was used.

Good agreement across NHLR, Wikipedia (citing the NRHP nomination), and Recreation.gov. No source gives an exact date for when staffing ended besides 'approximately 1946' or exactly when restoration occurred, only that it was 'abandoned for a number of years' before restoration.

Staffing conflicts: the register's October 2012 visit report says staffed sometimes and used in emergencies; the undated Chronicle feature says regularly manned; the smokejumper article (undated, refers to 2012 as past) says staffed in high fire danger. Story reports all three; facts.staffing uses the 2012 register statement. Height: 41 ft (register, firelookout.com) vs 40 ft (Chronicle, Montana Lookouts); height_m 12.5 is 41 ft converted. Elevation: record 2094.6 m matches the register's 6,872 ft; firelookout.com and the Chronicle give 7,077 ft. Record left unchanged. The register's description calls it Horse Mountain Lookout in one sentence, a name slip. Current access and climbability not verified on site. No photos added.

The brief's 'built: 1924' field is likely referring to the original pole-platform predecessor, not the structure now standing (built 1933); flagged as a correction. The current staffing claim comes only from firelookout.com, a hobbyist site with no visible date on that claim, so it is not strongly corroborated -- an NPS source confirming present-day staffing would strengthen this. Did not attempt to retrieve the NRHP nomination PDF itself (npgallery asset page returned only a metadata summary, not the full nomination text) or the NHLR newspaper-article PDF due to the per-tower read budget. Editorial pass 2026-10-04 fixed two footnote misattributions in the story: the 1924 pole-platform/log-cabin sentence was cited to Wikipedia ([^2]) but that detail is only in firelookout.com ([^3]); the 'chain of staffed fire lookouts' sentence was cited to NHLR ([^1]) but the quote is on Wikipedia ([^2]). The NRHP+NHLR registration sentence was missing a [^2] cite for the NRHP facts.

Two registrations share the name Jocko #2. This record (NHLR US 1543) is the standing 1969 CSKT R-6 timber tower. FFLOS US 2089 is a different 1934 Forest Service steel tower, removed, with footings only; keep them apart. Access level 'permission' in the record is not supported by any page read; it is left out of facts and should be treated as unverified. County (Missoula vs Lake) and elevation (7,636 vs 7,769 ft) conflict across sources. Staffing comes from an undated CSKT page. Leads not read: nwmt-ffla.org (Northwest Montana Lookout Association, lists historic, staffed and rental lookouts) and the CSKT preservation page. Page-read budget was used up, so no physical-state check was done.

Staffing: the register says semi-regularly staffed since 2001; firelookout.com says only that it was staffed in 2001. Access and rental not verified. Elevation: register 8,214 ft (2,504 m), firelookout.com 8284 ft; record 2503.6 m follows the register. The Powell County blog gives its newspaper quote as September 17, 1957 and then cites the same paper as September 17, 1954; the story says so. The Flathead NF Facebook lookout profile could not be read (page returned only its title), so it is not cited. A Forest Service Wikimedia Commons photo is geotagged about 60 m from the lookout, but the page does not say what the image shows, so no photo was added. Wikipedia says the 1957 lookout replaced a cabin of 1937, consistent with the register; it was used as a lead only.

The brief says the NHLR record shares a register number with another entry (US 1114, MT 62). Check for a duplicate record. Elevation conflicts (3,783 ft in NHLR vs 4943 ft on firelookout.com), and the record keeps the NHLR figure. Height correction: 15.2 m is 50 ft, the 1934 tower's height; the present 53-ft tower is about 16.2 m. The firelookout.com page is undated and says the tower is available for emergencies; the 2026 assessment says current access is closed for grizzly habitat. Do not encourage visiting. The 2026 condition assessment PDF linked from the NWMT page was not opened.

The 1977 build date is well supported and corrects the brief's 1969 build event. Staffing conflicts between NHLR (not regularly staffed) and the 2017 chapter report (DNRC part time); the as-of date is 2017. Current access is unconfirmed; no visiting or rental program found. height_m 6.1 converts the reported 20 feet of cab height, which is an inference from two sources. The 2016 Whitefish article calls Little Napa an L-4 design lookout in passing; design was not recorded because no source states it directly. One WebSearch was used. Five page reads.

Build date is genuinely unsettled across sources, including within Wikipedia's own article. No staffing history or fire history found beyond the disputed earlier-cabin-fire claim from firelookout.com.

Record's 2023 event cites nwmt-ffla.org/2023/09/01/2023-projects/, whose cached text is an empty shell; the Lost Horse assessment is in the NMLA 2023 Year-End Report PDF (source 2), so that source URL should be updated. Elevation differs: NHLR gives 6,523 ft (1,988 m), firelookout.com 6,558 ft; the record keeps the NHLR value. The access level 'restricted' is my reading of the flagged-route and no-road descriptions, not an official status; check with the Kootenai NF. No source gives the abandonment year or any staffing.

The brief flags a register-number conflict ('They share a register number'), presumably with another lookout in the dataset; none of the three sources read here gave any indication McCart's NHLR number (US 85) is wrong, so this could not be resolved from these pages and should be checked against whichever other record shares the number.

The brief flagged a register-number conflict ('They share a register number') but none of the three sources checked here show a shared/duplicate NHLR number; US 345 appears specific to McGuire on both NHLR and the firelookout.org list. That conflict may concern a source not checked in this pass. No source gives a specific fire credited to this lookout, or the exact date staffing began. Fact-check 2026-10-04: the draft's sentence on the 1923/1924 build-year split misattributed the dates, crediting Recreation.gov with the 1924 figure (it actually gives 1923, per source 2) and leaving firelookout.com unnamed as one of the two sources giving 1924; corrected. The physical-description sentence (pyramidal roof, cupola, interior ladder) cited only sources 1 and 3, but that detail comes from source 2's quote, so source 2 was added to the citation. A sentence claiming the lookout sat on 'Lincoln National Forest' land before the area became Kootenai National Forest was removed -- no source (and no real Forest Service unit near Eureka, MT) supports that name; it appears to be a mix-up with 'Lincoln Mountain,' which is actually part of the unrelated Garnet Mountain story in this same batch.

firelookout.com (source 3) corroborates the 1928/1936/1957 construction sequence but was not directly footnoted in the story since Recreation.gov already covers it in more detail; kept as a cross-check source. Fact-check 2026-10-04: the story had described the current cab as a '14-by-14-foot' tower; the Recreation.gov page actually gives a 225-square-foot cabin with no 14x14 dimension stated, so the story was corrected to match the source.

Build year is genuinely unresolved between NHLR (1930/1933) and firelookout.com (1940); the NRHP nomination's 'significant years' field (1939) was only partially legible in the crawl cache and did not include a clear text statement to resolve it, so I did not treat it as deciding the question. Firelookout.com's staffing list also includes a 1958 Mr. and Mrs. Dale Dye entry that had been omitted from the story; added it for completeness.

History from 1957 to 2018 is well sourced by the NRHP nomination. Present-day status and access rest on the nomination (form dated November 2, 2017), not a 2026 check; confirm with the Missoula Ranger District before publishing. Access level public is an inference from hikers visiting, not a posted status. height_m 16.2 is converted from 53 ft. firelookout.com's county and elevation are wrong or disputed. No photos added. Fact-check 2026-10-08: story reworded where it copied source wording, 'now serves' changed to the 2017 nomination's date, and evidence added for the 2006 shop move, the kit, the Missoula County claim and the vacancy.

Middle-tower date conflict (1950s vs 1968) not resolvable from available sources; flagged in story and resolved_conflicts. No NRHP nomination found for this tower. Fact-check 2026-10-04: the 'named for Col. David Minton' and 'first tower, 1932' sentences were mis-cited to source 1 (NHLR); that page does not contain either sentence verbatim (it instead says the original pole tower 'was replaced by an L-4 cab in 1932'). Both sentences are verbatim on source 2 (firelookout.com), and the Minton-name sentence is also verbatim on source 3 (Recreation.gov); citations corrected and the unsupported 'by the early 2000s the old tower was gone' claim was removed from the story.
Brief's conflict note about differing build years is explained by NHLR's own description distinguishing the 1921 platform from the 1959 cab; no discrepancy found between the three sources checked.
Conflict between NHLR (active until 1999) and recreation.gov/firelookout.com (unused since the 1970s) noted in the story and in resolved_conflicts; genuinely unresolved from the sources checked here.

Good staffing detail (Mathenys, last staffed 1971) and a notable 2017 Sprague Fire protection event, but sources don't describe the fire's actual approach/outcome for the structure beyond the wrap being installed.

Abandonment year conflicts (1973 vs 1978); both are stated in the story. Elevation differs across four sources; record kept. The record's 2016 assessed event is not supported by any source I read. The record's 2023 note mentions 'a few panes', which I did not find in the 2023 report text. Tower described as log (NHLR, 2026 page), pole (firelookout.com) and timber (Forest Lookouts page). The 1910 camp lookout appears only on firelookout.com. Access level 'restricted' is inferred from emergency-only use, not an official status. Register's 'Mt. Henry' 1973 text contains the typo 'n 1973' as printed.

The brief's 1932 build and 1972 abandonment hold. The 1921 camp date reconciles the build-year conflict in the brief. The brief's kind ground is not supported by any page read, so it was not recorded. Current condition after the 2025 assessment is not confirmed: only the report excerpt was read. The 2000 fire is recorded as a threat only; no source says it burned. Four page reads and one WebSearch used.

Restoration date conflict: register and 2026 summary say restored in the 1980s; firelookout.com says restoration took place through 2000. Both are in the story. Elevation: register 7,606 ft (2,318 m, matches record) vs firelookout.com 7705 ft. The 2024 date for the window removal is inferred from 'started last year' in the 2025 newsletter. Record events 2016 (field assessment), 2018 (new shutters), 2022 (very good shape) and the 2024 pre-project assessment were not found in the pages I read and are left out of this research file; check them before publishing. Access status is not in any source; no access key was set. The 2026 projects page says the project is rescheduled to 2027; any 2026 date in the record should be checked against it. Story no longer calls the site rocky (no source says so) and no longer says a reporter visited (the article gives only the August 10, 2025 date and photo credits).
Built-year discrepancy (1933 vs 1934) left unresolved per sources; worth a look at the NPGallery NRHP PDF (86000357) if a firmer date is wanted.

NHLR and FirelookOut share nearly the same wording, so the 1923, 1925 and 1962 dates rest mainly on one text, with the 1962 date backed by the independent 2022 magazine article. No NRHP nomination or Forest Service document was found or read. The access level is unknown: staffed in summer and reached by trail, but no source says whether the cab is open to visitors. The brief's record checked out on coordinates, elevation (within the NHLR figure), and the 1962 build date; no corrections. Fact-check 2026-10-08: the story's window wording now reads fragile piece, to match the 2022 magazine quote; the summit wording now reads lookout site, because the sources say here; and the visitor-access sentence no longer carries a footnote, since no cited source addresses it.

The original site and the first build date are unknown in every source read. The record's access level 'permission' is not confirmed: the tribal page and NHLR say nothing about visitors, and a Facebook group post that mentions a tribal permit could not be opened, so it is not cited. Access is set to unknown. Most history comes from the Register and a 1929/1947 newspaper excerpt quoted on the Forest Lookouts page; the 1947 article is not checked against the original paper. Lead for later: any Concord or Loudon city or town record that confirms the tower's ownership and public access.

The Register and the 1914 and 1930 items are consistent on the first steel tower, the 1971 raise and the 1976 cab. Current staffing is unconfirmed. Good corroboration across a historical register, a period newspaper quote (Courier-Post, 1940), the Wikipedia tower-list table, and a 2024 news feature confirming the tower is still actively staffed; all of those checked out against their cited sources. One claim did not hold up on cross-check: NHLR's Blue Anchor page says the original Aermotor tower was relocated to Stokes State Forest in 1932 to become 'the Culver tower,' but NHLR's own page for that lookout (Culvers Lookout, US44/NJ1) dates its present 47-ft Aermotor tower to 1933 and never mentions Blue Anchor — so the 'same tower, still standing at Stokes' claim in the earlier draft was an overclaim, now softened and the discrepancy disclosed in the story. Also removed an invented 'winter of 1920-21' detail not supported by the cited annual-report quote. No source found on public climbing access, so access.level was left unchanged rather than guessed.

Staffing as_of is the April 2023 visit report; no newer staffing data found. Access level 'restricted' is inferred from active status and the locked cab. The 1925 clipping's lookout details (season opening, visitor counts) are not used as Budd Lake events because the location conflicts. Brief height 18.0 m matches the register's 60 ft.

The 1916-1919 history comes from 1916-1919 newspaper and state report clippings reprinted on the Forest Lookouts page. The 1924 state tower and the 1946 addition come from the NHLR page only. Fact-check pass (2026-10-04) found three sourcing errors, now fixed: (1) the story cited Wikipedia for the claim that the CCC built an original 1936 lookout later rebuilt in 1940, but Wikipedia only says 'completed in 1940' and never mentions 1936 — the 1936/1940 two-stage claim is supported by Living New Deal (now added as source 5) and the USFS page, not Wikipedia, which now cites only the 1940 date alongside NHLR. (2) The New Mexico State Register of Cultural Properties claim was cited to the NPGallery NRHP record, which does not mention the state register at all; that fact is supported by Wikipedia (source 2, which gives the exact date March 4, 1988 and State Register No. 1445) and has been re-cited and split into its own event. (3) The story claimed Monjeau was 'the first lookout entered into the National Historic Lookout Register' outright; NHLR's own page says only that it was 'the first NHLR listing in New Mexico' — corrected to match. Did not find the NRHP nomination PDF text itself (only the NPGallery metadata page), so architectural/material description beyond NHLR's dimensions is thinner than ideal. No source found addressing current (2026) staffing beyond the 2007 volunteer visit report, which found it unstaffed with water damage and a stalled restoration contract; NHLR's current page description separately calls the lookout 'still in active use' as a visitor destination, which is about recreational use rather than fire-watch staffing and does not contradict the 2007 report.

The 2025-2026 renovation status rests on a trail guide (Komoot, last updated February 2026) and an FFLA project list; no town notice was found. The brief's coordinates (42.1039, -75.226733) sit several hundred metres from Wikipedia's tower coordinates (42 06 14 N, 75 13 06 W) and from the Tower Mountain summit (42.10944, -75.22611); not changed, so check the pin. No notable fire was found in these sources. The trail length of 3.9 miles from Komoot is not used. Grokipedia and a video appeared in search results and were not used.

The 35 ft height is the NHLR figure and the only height found; the LS-40 model name is not explained in any source read, so height_m 10.7 is unverified. The NHLR note describing a removed Bald Mountain tower near Old Forge conflicts with the other sources and needs an editor's check. The NHLR claim that the tower is on the National Register is unverified; NPGallery was not read. Andy Arthur pages returned HTTP 403 and were not used. The 15,000-visitor figure is from Wikipedia alone, and the 'more than 30 observers' figure is from a blog. Adirondack Explorer does not give a date for its article.

The brief's andyarthur.org page for Snowy returned HTTP 403 and was not readable. Its claims of a 1923 observer's cabin, a 2011 restoration led by Greg George, and the July 2024 fencing being completed are therefore unverified. The 1923 cabin is not in facts or events. The 2011 and 2024 items are corrected above because NHLR, the 2005 FFLA report and the April 2024 newsletter conflict with them. The NRHP nomination PDF is not digitized per NPGallery, so only its record metadata was used. Height is unresolved: NHLR implies about 42 ft, Wikipedia says 45 ft; 12.8 m is used with the conflict recorded. NHLR's photo (courtesy Laurie Rankin, Feb 2018) was not added because no image URL was found. The 2004 FFLA report lists the restored towers in prose and does not state a date for Snowy's restoration.

The historical record (1928 build, 1988 last staffing, 2014-2015 restoration) is consistent across DEC, NHLR, Saratoga PLAN and SummitPost. The current closure of the tower comes from a Saratoga PLAN page that cites DEC; no date for the structural closure was found, so re-check before publishing. The brief's staffing and access fields were unknown; the 2017 NHLR visit reports say unstaffed. Wikipedia says the tower is one of only 23 remaining in the Adirondacks, and Saratoga PLAN says the park has 25 mountains with towers; neither is used. No notable fire was found in these sources.

The Friends history is the main source and is a local-group account that cites Fred Knauf's history; the dates it gives for the observer, the 1918 tower, the 1990 closure, the 2014 management plan and the 2016 reopening agree with NHLR and the Adirondack Explorer. Open point: NHLR's 1909 site date versus the Friends' April 1910 observer date. The NRHP nomination PDF was not read. The Explorer's 6.6-mile round-trip figure from the main trailhead was not used. No photos were added; NHLR credits Bill Starr and David Petrelli for its photos, but their licences were not checked.

Story is built on the register page, the Forest Lookouts page, two NYS chapter documents, a 2006 radio log and the NPS record. Closure start date is not in any source read; the 2023 event year is the report date, not the closure date. The brief's 2017 closure, 2019 cab-window work and 2022 inspection-completed events were not verified in sources read and are left out. The chapter's annual report file is named cr-ny-2023 but its header reads Annual Report 2024; its content covers 2023. Agency correction (DEC to NY State Parks) needs confirming with OPRHP or NY State Parks. The register calls the listing a Federal Register placement; the story says 'historic register' for the June 12, 2006 date and cites the NPS National Register record for the 7/28/2006 publication date. The 2006 radio log's author is not identified. A fresh check of the tower's current status (reopening or inspection result) is advisable before publication.

Seasonal closure: the DEC map says the trail and summit close from the second Tuesday in October through December 20. Our count puts the 2026 start at Tuesday October 13, which is five days after the research date. Confirm with DEC or the Friends before anyone plans a visit. The Friends' homepage banner (closed until December 20, 2025) is stale. The record's 2017 NRHP listing is not confirmed: the Explorer reports only that the state nominated the structure, and the NRHP nomination PDF was not read. The 1882 Colvin tower rests on one source (the Explorer); the Forest Lookouts page and the Register begin in 1912 and do not mention it. Trail length differs: 1.2 miles (DEC) vs one mile (Explorer, Friends). Staffing is from a December 2017 Register visit report only; no current staffing was found. No photos added. The Explorer photo credit (Nancy Ford) is not reusable without permission. Pages read: 8 (including one 403 that failed) plus two web searches; the Explorer and DEC map were read last and carry the access and history claims.

Only two sources could be read. The Friends of Stissing Landmarks site (stissingfiretower.org/history and the home page) rendered no text, and the New Pine Plains Herald article on the stair and landing replacement (completed October 24, year not visible) returned no body text, so neither is cited. The nysffla.org fire tower list returned 404 on the URL tried, and a search showed an alphabetical list at nysffla.org/alphalist.html that was not read. The story stops at the page-read budget. The register and Wikipedia conflict on the build year (1933 vs 1934), the height (86 ft vs 79 ft 6 in), and the end of lookout service (April 1971 vs 1979-1982). Those are unresolved and need the FOSL history page, the Herald article, or the nysffla list to settle. The register's 2017-2018 restoration is described as expected, so current completion is unverified. The story does not state the restored tower's current hours. The brief's events are kept as they stand: '1934 built' is supported by the register's Built field and the opening date, and the Wikipedia date is noted as a conflict.

The DEC notice says the tower is closed; the crawl date of that page is unknown, so confirm with DEC Region 8 before publishing as current. The CNY Hiking and Wikipedia access text is undated. The NHLR credits DEC Region 8 staff with preserving the 1941 cabin, but no current cabin status was verified. The NY Almanack 2026 article (consistently staffed until the 1980s) was seen only in search and grep output and was not used as a citation.

Design model disagrees: the register says LS-47, the 2023 FFLA grant report says LS-40. The brief's 2024 entries (interpretive panels added by Warren County; a roof panel installed before an Aug. 31 lighting event) were not found in any source I read, so they are left out; the roof work's completion is unconfirmed. The register's Administered-by line (NYS DEC) conflicts with the 2021 news report (Warren County owns it); the agency correction is for human review. Post-Star article date is not shown in the text I read, so it is cited only for the trail opening and the 47-foot height. No staffing or climbing status sources were found. Access is public per the 2021 news report, which is five years old; check current status before relying on it. One WebSearch call and eight page reads used on this lookout.

Dates for the move are the weakest part. The register says late 1990s; Wikipedia says the rebuild began in the 1980s, the cab was finished in 1999 and the tower was dedicated in July 2000; a 1982 newspaper shows erection under way. Wikipedia cites a 2021 Adirondack Mountain Club book and a NYSFFLA list that were not checked. The 1971 removal rests on Wikipedia alone. The 47-foot height is given without a cab-floor figure, so height_m is left out. The record's 'relocated' event had no year; 1982 is the first dated mention, not the move date. The sister record us-ny-tooley-pond-mountain carries an unverified location (44.27104, -74.93038) that these sources do not confirm. Current access is unverified beyond the register's wording. The Adirondack Explorer hike write-up (cite 5) also dates the reassembly to 2000; the story does not give that date.

Dates and height conflict across sources (closure 1971 vs 1975; 47 ft vs 65 ft in a 1917 item). The Catskill Center page is undated, so staffing as_of is the year only. Andy Arthur pages returned HTTP 403 and were not used. The NHLR photo (Feb 2016, courtesy of Laurie Rankin) has no licence or URL, so no photo was added. The brief's access 'unknown' is now public based on the Catskill Center and marker.

Core dates (1934 build, 1989 end of service, village ownership, 2004-05 restoration, 2015 registration) agree across the Register, the FFLA and Wikipedia. Conflicts are recorded in resolved_conflicts. The 1933 newspaper report on Forest Lookouts names a 60-foot steel tower to be completed in September 1933, so the 1934 build year is the consensus, not a certainty. The Register's visit report is dated October 21, 2017 (Laurie Rankin); its 'needs paint' and 'good overall condition' lines come from that visit, so they are nine years old as of 2026. The brief's agency (NYSDEC) is corrected to village ownership. No photo was added: the Register's photo is credited to Laurie Rankin (Oct 2017) and no image URL was retrieved. The brief's andyarthur.org page for the summit (p/216687) was not read.

The end of fire watch conflicts (1971 NHLR vs 1988 Wikipedia), and whether the cab is open to visitors is unconfirmed. Recommend a DEC check before the story is published as safe-to-visit. The brief's elevation (1,013.5 m) is the NHLR tower-site figure, not the summit. The AARCH item is a columnar newspaper PDF, so quotes are short fragments. Facebook group posts about the 1911 wood tower were not used. The Andy Arthur page was not used. No photo added.

Sources disagree on the closure cause and date (NHLR: footing deterioration, December 2016; DEC: wind damage in winter 2017) and on the number of footings (NHLR: 8 repaired in June 2018; DEC: 4 replaced). Height is 72 ft per NHLR and 70 ft per DEC, so height_m is left out. The DEC release is undated in the cached copy; its reopening is placed by the June 2018 NHLR entry. No closure notice after 2018 was found; the newest visitor report read is from 2022. Current access should be checked before publication. The 1955 newspaper and 1960 donation facts come from the Forest Lookouts page, which quotes newspapers without links. The DEC announcement is undated in the cache, so the story reports it as the state's announcement rather than as current status.
